                {
                  "lineNumber": 8,
                  "content": "# Skill Creator"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 10,
                  "content": "This skill provides guidance for creating effective skills."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 12,
                  "content": "## About Skills"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 14,
                  "content": "Skills are modular, self-contained packages that extend Codex's capabilities by providing"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 19,
                  "content": "### What Skills Provide"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 30,
                  "content": "The context window is a public good. Skills share the context window with everything else Codex needs: system prompt, conversation history, other Skills' metadata, and the actual user request."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 48,
                  "content": "### Anatomy of a Skill"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 50,
                  "content": "Every skill consists of a required SKILL.md file and optional bundled resources:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 53,
                  "content": "skill-name/"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 54,
                  "content": "├── SKILL.md (required)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 65,
                  "content": "#### SKILL.md (required)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 67,
                  "content": "Every SKILL.md consists of:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 69,
                  "content": "- **Frontmatter** (YAML): Contains &#96;name&#96; and &#96;description&#96; fields. These are the only fields that Codex reads to determine when the skill gets used, thus it is very important to be clear and comprehensive in describing what the skill is, and when it should be used."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 70,
                  "content": "- **Body** (Markdown): Instructions and guidance for using the skill. Only loaded AFTER the skill triggers (if at all)."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 90,
                  "content": "- **Benefits**: Keeps SKILL.md lean, loaded only when Codex determines it's needed"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 91,
                  "content": "- **Best practice**: If files are large (&gt;10k words), include grep search patterns in SKILL.md"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 92,
                  "content": "- **Avoid duplication**: Information should live in either SKILL.md or references files, not both. Prefer references files for detailed information unless it's truly core to the skill—this keeps SKILL.md lean while making information discoverable without hogging the context window. Keep only essential procedural instructions and workflow guidance in SKILL.md; move detailed reference material, schemas, and examples to references files."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 98,
                  "content": "- **When to include**: When the skill needs files that will be used in the final output"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 103,
                  "content": "#### What to Not Include in a Skill"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 105,
                  "content": "A skill should only contain essential files that directly support its functionality. Do NOT create extraneous documentation or auxiliary files, including:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 113,
                  "content": "The skill should only contain the information needed for an AI agent to do the job at hand. It should not contain auxiliary context about the process that went into creating it, setup and testing procedures, user-facing documentation, etc. Creating additional documentation files just adds clutter and confusion."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 117,
                  "content": "Skills use a three-level loading system to manage context efficiently:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 120,
                  "content": "2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill triggers (&lt;5k words)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 125,
                  "content": "Keep SKILL.md body to the essentials and under 500 lines to minimize context bloat. Split content into separate files when approaching this limit. When splitting out content into other files, it is very important to reference them from SKILL.md and describe clearly when to read them, to ensure the reader of the skill knows they exist and when to use them."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 127,
                  "content": "**Key principle:** When a skill supports multiple variations, frameworks, or options, keep only the core workflow and selection guidance in SKILL.md. Move variant-specific details (patterns, examples, configuration) into separate reference files."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 150,
                  "content": "For Skills with multiple domains, organize content by domain to avoid loading irrelevant context:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 153,
                  "content": "bigquery-skill/"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 154,
                  "content": "├── SKILL.md (overview and navigation)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 164,
                  "content": "Similarly, for skills supporting multiple frameworks or variants, organize by variant:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 168,
                  "content": "├── SKILL.md (workflow + provider selection)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 200,
                  "content": "- **Avoid deeply nested references** - Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md. All reference files should link directly from SKILL.md."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 203,
                  "content": "## Skill Creation Process"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 205,
                  "content": "Skill creation involves these steps:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 207,
                  "content": "1. Understand the skill with concrete examples"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 208,
                  "content": "2. Plan reusable skill contents (scripts, references, assets)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 209,
                  "content": "3. Initialize the skill (run init_skill.py)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 210,
                  "content": "4. Edit the skill (implement resources and write SKILL.md)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 211,
                  "content": "5. Package the skill (run package_skill.py)"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 216,
                  "content": "### Skill Naming"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 222,
                  "content": "- Name the skill folder exactly after the skill name."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 224,
                  "content": "### Step 1: Understanding the Skill with Concrete Examples"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 226,
                  "content": "Skip this step only when the skill's usage patterns are already clearly understood. It remains valuable even when working with an existing skill."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 228,
                  "content": "To create an effective skill, clearly understand concrete examples of how the skill will be used. This understanding can come from either direct user examples or generated examples that are validated with user feedback."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 230,
                  "content": "For example, when building an image-editor skill, relevant questions include:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 232,
                  "content": "- \"What functionality should the image-editor skill support? Editing, rotating, anything else?\""
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 233,
                  "content": "- \"Can you give some examples of how this skill would be used?\""
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 234,
                  "content": "- \"I can imagine users asking for things like 'Remove the red-eye from this image' or 'Rotate this image'. Are there other ways you imagine this skill being used?\""
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 235,
                  "content": "- \"What would a user say that should trigger this skill?\""
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 239,
                  "content": "Conclude this step when there is a clear sense of the functionality the skill should support."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 241,
                  "content": "### Step 2: Planning the Reusable Skill Contents"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 243,
                  "content": "To turn concrete examples into an effective skill, analyze each example by:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 248,
                  "content": "Example: When building a &#96;pdf-editor&#96; skill to handle queries like \"Help me rotate this PDF,\" the analysis shows:"
                },

                  "lineNumber": 251,
                  "content": "2. A &#96;scripts/rotate_pdf.py&#96; script would be helpful to store in the skill"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 253,
                  "content": "Example: When designing a &#96;frontend-webapp-builder&#96; skill for queries like \"Build me a todo app\" or \"Build me a dashboard to track my steps,\" the analysis shows:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 256,
                  "content": "2. An &#96;assets/hello-world/&#96; template containing the boilerplate HTML/React project files would be helpful to store in the skill"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 258,
                  "content": "Example: When building a &#96;big-query&#96; skill to handle queries like \"How many users have logged in today?\" the analysis shows:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 261,
                  "content": "2. A &#96;references/schema.md&#96; file documenting the table schemas would be helpful to store in the skill"

                {
                  "lineNumber": 302,

                  "lineNumber": 307,
                  "content": "These files contain established best practices for effective skill design."

                {
                  "lineNumber": 309,
                  "content": "#### Start with Reusable Skill Contents"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 311,

                  "content": "        \"contents\": \"# Skills (experimental)\\n\\n&amp;gt; **Warning:** This is an experimental and non-stable feature. If you depend on it, please expect breaking changes over the coming weeks and understand that there is currently no guarantee that this works well. Use at your own risk!\\n\\nCodex can automatically discover reusable \\\"skills\\\" you keep on disk. A skill is a small bundle with a name, a short description (what it does and when to use it), and an optional body of instructions you can open when needed. Codex injects only the name, description, and file path into the runtime context; the body stays on disk.\\n\\n## Enable skills\\n\\nSkills are behind the experimental &amp;#96;skills&amp;#96; feature flag and are disabled by default.\\n\\n- Enable in config (preferred): add the following to &amp;#96;$CODEX_HOME/config.toml&amp;#96; (usually &amp;#96;~/.codex/config.toml&amp;#96;) and restart Codex:\\n\\n  &amp;#96;&amp;#96;&amp;#96;toml\\n  [features]\\n  skills = true\\n  &amp;#96;&amp;#96;&amp;#96;\\n\\n- Enable for a single run: launch Codex with &amp;#96;codex --enable skills&amp;#96;\\n\\n## Where skills live\\n\\n- Location (v1): &amp;#96;~/.codex/skills/**/SKILL.md&amp;#96; (recursive). Hidden entries and symlinks are skipped. Only files named exactly &amp;#96;SKILL.md&amp;#96; count.\\n- Sorting: rendered by name, then path for stability.\\n\\n## File format\\n\\n- YAML frontmatter + body.\\n  - Required:\\n    - &amp;#96;name&amp;#96; (non-empty, ≤100 chars, sanitized to one line)\\n    - &amp;#96;description&amp;#96; (non-empty, ≤500 chars, sanitized to one line)\\n  - Extra keys are ignored. The body can contain any Markdown; it is not injected into context.\\n\\n## Loading and rendering\\n\\n- Loaded once at startup.\\n- If valid skills exist, Codex appends a runtime-only &amp;#96;## Skills&amp;#96; section after &amp;#96;AGENTS.md&amp;#96;, one bullet per skill: &amp;#96;- &amp;lt;name&amp;gt;: &amp;lt;description&amp;gt; (file: /absolute/path/to/SKILL.md)&amp;#96;.\\n- If no valid skills exist, the section is omitted. On-disk files are never modified.\\n\\n## Using skills\\n\\n- Mention a skill by name in a message using &amp;#96;$&amp;lt;skill-name&amp;gt;&amp;#96;.\\n- In the TUI, you can also use &amp;#96;/skills&amp;#96; to browse and insert skills.\\n\\n## Validation and errors\\n\\n- Invalid skills (missing/invalid YAML, empty/over-length fields) trigger a blocking, dismissible startup modal in the TUI that lists each path and error. Errors are also logged. You can dismiss to continue (invalid skills are ignored) or exit. Fix SKILL.md files and restart to clear the modal.\\n\\n## Create a skill\\n\\n1. Create &amp;#96;~/.codex/skills/&amp;lt;skill-name&amp;gt;/&amp;#96;.\","

                  "content": "        \"contents\": \"use std::collections::HashMap;\\nuse std::path::Path;\\nuse std::path::PathBuf;\\nuse std::sync::RwLock;\\n\\nuse crate::skills::SkillLoadOutcome;\\nuse crate::skills::loader::load_skills_from_roots;\\nuse crate::skills::loader::skill_roots_for_cwd;\\nuse crate::skills::system::install_system_skills;\\npub struct SkillsManager {\\n    codex_home: PathBuf,\\n    cache_by_cwd: RwLock&amp;lt;HashMap&amp;lt;PathBuf, SkillLoadOutcome&amp;gt;&amp;gt;,\\n}\\n\\nimpl SkillsManager {\\n    pub fn new(codex_home: PathBuf) -&amp;gt; Self {\\n        if let Err(err) = install_system_skills(&amp;amp;codex_home) {\\n            tracing::error!(\\\"failed to install system skills: {err}\\\");\\n        }\\n\\n        Self {\\n            codex_home,\\n            cache_by_cwd: RwLock::new(HashMap::new()),\\n        }\\n    }\\n\\n    pub fn skills_for_cwd(&amp;amp;self, cwd: &amp;amp;Path) -&amp;gt; SkillLoadOutcome {\\n        self.skills_for_cwd_with_options(cwd, false)\\n    }\\n\\n    pub fn skills_for_cwd_with_options(&amp;amp;self, cwd: &amp;amp;Path, force_reload: bool) -&amp;gt; SkillLoadOutcome {\\n        let cached = match self.cache_by_cwd.read() {\\n            Ok(cache) =&amp;gt; cache.get(cwd).cloned(),\\n            Err(err) =&amp;gt; err.into_inner().get(cwd).cloned(),\\n        };\\n        if !force_reload &amp;amp;&amp;amp; let Some(outcome) = cached {\\n            return outcome;\\n        }\\n\\n        let roots = skill_roots_for_cwd(&amp;amp;self.codex_home, cwd);\\n        let outcome = load_skills_from_roots(roots);\\n        match self.cache_by_cwd.write() {\\n            Ok(mut cache) =&amp;gt; {\\n                cache.insert(cwd.to_path_buf(), outcome.clone());\\n            }\\n            Err(err) =&amp;gt; {\\n                err.into_inner().insert(cwd.to_path_buf(), outcome.clone());\\n            }\\n        }\\n        outcome\\n    }\\n}\","

                  "content": "        \"contents\": \"## Validation and errors\\n\\n- Invalid skills (missing/invalid YAML, empty/over-length fields) trigger a blocking, dismissible startup modal in the TUI that lists each path and error. Errors are also logged. You can dismiss to continue (invalid skills are ignored) or exit. Fix SKILL.md files and restart to clear the modal.\\n\\n## Create a skill\\n\\n1. Create &amp;#96;~/.codex/skills/&amp;lt;skill-name&amp;gt;/&amp;#96;.\\n2. Add &amp;#96;SKILL.md&amp;#96;:\\n\\n   &amp;#96;&amp;#96;&amp;#96;\\n   ---\\n   name: your-skill-name\\n   description: what it does and when to use it (&amp;lt;=500 chars)\\n   ---\\n\\n   # Optional body\\n   Add instructions, references, examples, or scripts (kept on disk).\\n   &amp;#96;&amp;#96;&amp;#96;\\n\\n3. Keep &amp;#96;name&amp;#96;/&amp;#96;description&amp;#96; within the limits; avoid newlines in those fields.\\n4. Restart Codex to load the new skill.\\n\\n## Example\\n\\n&amp;#96;&amp;#96;&amp;#96;\\nmkdir -p ~/.codex/skills/pdf-processing\\ncat &amp;lt;&amp;lt;'SKILL_EXAMPLE' &amp;gt; ~/.codex/skills/pdf-processing/SKILL.md\\n---\\nname: pdf-processing\\ndescription: Extract text and tables from PDFs; use when PDFs, forms, or document extraction are mentioned.\\n---\\n\\n# PDF Processing\\n- Use pdfplumber to extract text.\\n- For form filling, see FORMS.md.\\nSKILL_EXAMPLE\\n&amp;#96;&amp;#96;&amp;#96;\","

                  "content": "        \"contents\": \"## Slash Commands\\n\\n### What are slash commands?\\n\\nSlash commands are special commands you can type that start with &amp;#96;/&amp;#96;.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Built-in slash commands\\n\\nControl Codex’s behavior during an interactive session with slash commands.\\n\\n| Command         | Purpose                                                                    |\\n| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\\n| &amp;#96;/model&amp;#96;        | choose what model and reasoning effort to use                              |\\n| &amp;#96;/approvals&amp;#96;    | choose what Codex can do without approval                                  |\\n| &amp;#96;/review&amp;#96;                   "lineNumber": 12918,
                  "content": "        \"contents\": \"use crate::skills::model::SkillMetadata;\\n\\npub fn render_skills_section(skills: &amp;amp;[SkillMetadata]) -&amp;gt; Option&amp;lt;String&amp;gt; {\\n    if skills.is_empty() {\\n        return None;\\n    }\\n\\n    let mut lines: Vec&amp;lt;String&amp;gt; = Vec::new();\\n    lines.push(\\\"## Skills\\\".to_string());\\n    lines.push(\\\"These skills are discovered at startup from multiple local sources. Each entry includes a name, description, and file path so you can open the source for full instructions.\\\".to_string());\\n\\n    for skill in skills {\\n        let path_str = skill.path.to_string_lossy().replace('\\\\\\\\', \\\"/\\\");\\n        let name = skill.name.as_str();\\n        let description = skill.description.as_str();\\n        lines.push(format!(\\\"- {name}: {description} (file: {path_str})\\\"));\\n    }\\n\\n    lines.push(\\n        r###\\\"- Discovery: Available skills are listed in project docs and may also appear in a runtime \\\"## Skills\\\" section (name + description + file path). These are the sources of truth; skill bodies live on disk at the listed paths.\\n- Trigger rules: If the user names a skill (with &amp;#96;$SkillName&amp;#96; or plain text) OR the task clearly matches a skill's description, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.\\n- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.\\n- How to use a skill (progressive disclosure):\\n  1) After deciding to use a skill, open its &amp;#96;SKILL.md&amp;#96;. Read only enough to follow the workflow.\\n  2) If &amp;#96;SKILL.md&amp;#96; points to extra folders such as &amp;#96;references/&amp;#96;, load only the specific files needed for the request; don't bulk-load everything.\\n  3) If &amp;#96;scripts/&amp;#96; exist, prefer running or patching them instead of retyping large code blocks.\\n  4) If &amp;#96;assets/&amp;#96; or templates exist, reuse them instead of recreating from scratch.\\n- Description as trigger: The YAML &amp;#96;description&amp;#96; in &amp;#96;SKILL.md&amp;#96; is the primary trigger signal; rely on it to decide applicability. If unsure, ask a brief clarification before proceeding.\\n- Coordination and sequencing:\\n  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.\\n  - Announce which skill(s) you're using and why (one short line). If you skip an obvious skill, say why.\\n- Context hygiene:\\n  - Keep context small: summarize long sections instead of pasting them; only load extra files when needed.\\n  - Avoid deeply nested references; prefer one-hop files explicitly linked from &amp;#96;SKILL.md&amp;#96;.\\n  - When variants exist (frameworks, providers, domains), pick only the relevant reference file(s) and note that choice.\\n- Safety and fallback: If a skill can't be applied cleanly (missing files, unclear instructions), state the issue, pick the next-best approach, and continue.\\\"###\\n            .to_string(),\\n    );\\n\\n    Some(lines.join(\\\"\\\\n\\\"))\\n}\","

The performance gains are reflected in the latest industry benchmarks. GPT-5.2-Codex achieved a record-breaking 56.4% accuracy rate on SWE-Bench Pro, a rigorous test that requires models to resolve real-world GitHub issues within large, unfamiliar software environments. While its primary rival, Claude 4.5 Opus from Anthropic, maintains a slight lead on the SWE-Bench Verified set (80.9% vs. OpenAI’s 80.0%), GPT-5.2-Codex’s 64.0% score on Terminal-Bench 2.0 underscores its superior ability to navigate live terminal environments, compile code, and manage server configurations in real-time. Furthermore, the model’s vision capabilities have been significantly upgraded to support technical diagramming. GPT-5.2-Codex can now ingest architectural schematics, flowcharts, and even Figma UI mockups, translating them directly into functional React or Next.js prototypes. This multimodal reasoning allows the agent to identify structural logic flaws in system designs before a single line of code is even written, bridging the gap between high-level system architecture and low-level implementation. The Market Impact: Microsoft and the \"Agent Wars\" The release of GPT-5.2-Codex has immediate and profound implications for the tech industry, particularly for Microsoft ( NASDAQ: MSFT ), which remains OpenAI’s primary partner. By integrating this agentic model into the GitHub ecosystem, Microsoft is positioning itself to capture the lion's share of the enterprise developer market. Already, early adopters such as Cisco ( NASDAQ: CSCO ) and Duolingo ( NASDAQ: DUOL ) have reported integrating the model to accelerate their engineering pipelines, with some teams noting a 40% reduction in time-to-ship for complex features. Competitive pressure is mounting on other tech giants. Google ( NASDAQ: GOOGL ) continues to push its Gemini 3 Pro model, which boasts a 1-million-plus token context window, while Anthropic focuses on the superior \"reasoning and design\" capabilities of the Claude family. However, OpenAI’s strategic focus on \"agentic autonomy\"—the ability for a model to use tools, run tests, and self-correct without human intervention—gives it a distinct advantage in the burgeoning market for automated software maintenance. Startups in the AI-powered development space are also feeling the disruption. As GPT-5.2-Codex moves closer to performing the role of a junior-to-mid-level engineer, many existing \"wrapper\" companies that provide basic AI coding features may find their value propositions absorbed by the native capabilities of the OpenAI platform. The market is increasingly shifting toward \"agent orchestration\" platforms that can manage fleets of these autonomous coders across distributed teams. Cybersecurity Revolution and the CVE-2025-55182 Discovery One of the most striking aspects of the GPT-5.2-Codex launch is its demonstrated prowess in defensive cybersecurity. OpenAI highlighted a landmark case study involving the discovery and patching of CVE-2025-55182, a critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw known as \"React2Shell.\" While a predecessor model was used for the initial investigation, GPT-5.2-Codex has \"industrialized\" the process, leading to the discovery of three additional zero-day vulnerabilities: CVE-2025-55183 (source code exposure), CVE-2025-55184, and CVE-2025-67779 (a significant Denial of Service flaw). This leap in vulnerability detection has sparked a complex debate within the security community. While the model offers unprecedented speed for defensive teams seeking to patch systems, the \"dual-use\" risk is undeniable. The same reasoning that allows GPT-5.2-Codex to find and fix a bug can, in theory, be used to exploit it. In response to these concerns, OpenAI has launched an invite-only \"Trusted Access Pilot,\" providing vetted security professionals with access to the model’s most permissive features while maintaining strict monitoring for offensive misuse. This development mirrors previous milestones in AI safety and security, but the stakes are now significantly higher. As AI agents gain the ability to write and deploy code autonomously, the window for human intervention in cyberattacks is shrinking. The industry is now looking toward \"autonomous defense\" systems where AI agents like GPT-5.2-Codex constantly probe their own infrastructure for weaknesses, creating a perpetual cycle of automated hardening. The Road Ahead: Automated Maintenance and AGI in Engineering Looking toward 2026, the trajectory for GPT-5.2-Codex suggests a future where software \"maintenance\" as we know it is largely automated. Experts predict that the next iteration of the model will likely include native support for video-based UI debugging—allowing the AI to watch a user experience a bug in a web application and trace the error back through the stack to the specific line of code responsible. The long-term goal for OpenAI remains the achievement of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in the domain of software engineering. This would involve a model capable of not just following instructions, but identifying business needs and architecting entire software products from scratch with minimal human oversight. Challenges remain, particularly regarding the reliability of AI-generated code in safety-critical systems and the legal complexities of copyright and code ownership in an era of autonomous generation. However, the consensus among researchers is that the \"agentic\" hurdle has been cleared. We are no longer asking if an AI can manage a software project; we are now asking how many projects a single engineer can oversee when supported by a fleet of GPT-5.2-Codex agents. The coming months will be a crucial testing ground for these models as they are integrated into the production environments of the world's largest software companies. A Milestone in the History of Computing The launch of GPT-5.2-Codex is more than just a model update; it is a fundamental shift in the relationship between humans and computers. By achieving a 56.4% score on SWE-Bench Pro and demonstrating the capacity for autonomous vulnerability discovery, OpenAI has set a new standard for what \"agentic\" AI can achieve. The model’s ability to \"see\" technical diagrams and \"remember\" context over long-horizon tasks effectively removes many of the bottlenecks that have historically limited AI's utility in high-level engineering. As we move into 2026, the focus will shift from the raw capabilities of these models to their practical implementation and the safeguards required to manage them. For now, GPT-5.2-Codex stands as a testament to the rapid pace of AI development, signaling a future where the role of the human developer evolves from a writer of code to an orchestrator of intelligent agents. The tech world will be watching closely as the \"Trusted Access Pilot\" expands and the first wave of enterprise-scale autonomous migrations begins.
